articles.title: BRUCE PEARL: Conservatives are attacking the very college sports bill that protects women
articles.summary: Retired Auburn coach says critics wrongly claim the Protect College Sports Act guts Title IX, warning that inaction threatens women's and Olympic sports programs.
articles.body: Men don’t belong in women’s sports. That isn’t complicated, but some conservative influencers and interest groups are allowing it to become complicated through careless claims about legislation designed to protect college athletics. I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts and win the larger fight for women, fairness and the future of college sports. Some organizations and women’s-sports advocates claim the Protect College Sports Act would "gut" Title IX or invalidate state laws that reserve women’s teams for women. They are wrong. The text says the opposite. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: COLLEGE SPORTS BILL ENTERS LEGISLATIVE 'RED ZONE' AS SEASON KICKS OFF Section 127 explicitly states that nothing in the bill will "override, modify, or amend" Title IX. Female athletes would retain their current legal protections and ability to bring sex-discrimination claims. Section 120 also protects athletes, employees and others from retaliation for reporting discrimination or participating in Title IX proceedings. I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts. Critics also claim the bill would erase state laws keeping men out of women’s sports. It would not. The legislation establishes national standards for Division I and Division II competition on limited eligibility questions, including academics, professional status, legal violations, age and years of eligibility. It neither creates a federal right for men to enter women’s competitions nor pre-empts state laws establishing sex-based athletic categories. REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS The bill does not expressly create a federal right for biological males to compete in women’s sports, and Section 127 states that nothing in the bill overrides, modifies or amends Title IX. Critics seem to be grasping at anything and eager to disregard the Title IX provisions here. Especially since the Supreme Court ruled in June that schools may keep men out of women’s sports. It also requires governing bodies to enforce rules related to state and federal law and allows individuals to sue when the law is violated. CONGRESS MUST FIX THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE GIRLS PAY THE PRICE The bill also gives schools a powerful incentive to invest in women’s and Olympic sports. It creates a $22.5 million athlete-retention fund and allows schools to unlock up to an additional $5 million through eligible NIL investments in women’s, Olympic and non-revenue sports. A school seeking the full $27.5 million retention allowance would first need to invest $5 million in those sports. That is an ingenious way to ensure continued investment in programs that might otherwise be left behind. And every year Congress waits, the financial pressure on college athletics grows, and the programs with the fewest resources become even more vulnerable. My 2025 Final Four team had a total NIL budget of approximately $4 million. By the 2027 Final Four, some teams could be operating with budgets approaching $30 million. Conservatives should debate legislation, demand improvements and scrutinize every line. But facts must guide us. Too many Washington organizations would rather score points against perceived rivals than secure lasting victories for women and college athletes. CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION Outrage is easy; turning shared principles into law is harder. Infighting only helps the left, which has spent years undermining Title IX while conservatives battle over legislation that expressly preserves it. If we can’t unite and get this done, we will lose college sports as we know them, and women’s and Olympic sports will continue to be among the first casualties. The stakes extend beyond Title IX, and the crisis is no longer theoretical. Thirty-two Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between the announcement of the House settlement and May 2025. WRAL reported that more than 40 Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between May 2024 and July 2025, even though 75% of American Olympians in 2024 competed in collegiate athletics. NCAA data Even the University of Arkansas, backed by SEC resources, announced plans to eliminate its tennis programs before donors intervened to save them. If programs at schools like Arkansas are vulnerable, imagine the danger facing smaller schools, women’s teams and non-revenue sports nationwide. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Credit where credit is due: Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., and others have stepped up to move this legislation forward. President Trump has also led from the front by restoring the biological meaning of sex in federal policy, taking action to save college sports and backing this bill. Now, those who claim to support the America First movement should get in the game, help Congress finish the job and deliver this win for women and college athletes. Congress now has the opportunity to take important steps to stabilize college sports, support educational opportunities for young women and men, and provide protections for the uniquely American experience of intercollegiate athletics. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There is broad agreement that college sports cannot go on with no meaningful guardrails around eligibility, transfer policy and NIL oversight. The Protect College Sports Act is an important step in the right direction, and Congress needs to keep the positive momentum moving forward. Winning the point may feel good. Winning the war matters more.

articles.title: Graham hopes Trump propels her across finish line in South Carolina
articles.summary: The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.),…
articles.body:
The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who was tapped to serve out her brother’s term and whom Trump encouraged to run for another six years, and supporters of Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus with a long history of representing the state.

Trump has leaned into the race in a way he has rarely done this midterm cycle, holding a campaign rally Friday night in Myrtle Beach, S.C., for Graham and attaching his own political clout to the outcome.

“What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump told supporters at a rally for Graham Friday night in Myrtle Beach.

“So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time,” the president added. “You got to say it, and you got to come out and vote.”

Trump’s MAGA Inc. also spent over $827,000 for Graham, marking the super PAC’s first independent expenditure since March.

Graham’s support has come from establishment Republicans , including the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the president himself , political action committees and business executives. The Palmetto State’s governor, who appointed Graham to her brother’s seat , is campaigning with the senator on Monday.

Norman, meanwhile, has self-funded much of his campaign and has leaned on his conservative policy chops, while accusing Graham of being “controlled by the Washington elite.”

But with such a short campaign window and a limited public record to run on, every move Graham has made matters.

So during last week’s debate, when Graham struggled to answer a rudimentary question on foreign policy — a subject matter that came to define much of her late brother’s legacy in public service — the moment came to dominate the news cycle.

“That’s the kind of thing that, if she does lose on Tuesday, I feel like we’ll be chalking entirely up to that,” Geoffrey Skelley, Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst, said of the debate flub.

“Of course that would be simplistic, but if you’re not familiar, and you find yourself as the front-runner … that really stands out as a defining moment for your candidacy,” he continued. “You can see how she might end up blowing this.”

Norman has pledged not to go negative on the campaign against Graham, saying last week, “She’s been through a lot. … She really has, losing a brother. I’m not going to do that,” referring to his decision not to run antagonistic ads.

But the congressman has still highlighted Graham’s lack of political experience, both on the debate stage and in the days that followed.

“By her choice, she’s running for the United States Senate. It’s a six-year term,” Norman said during the debate. “You need to get fully versed in what issues you’re going to be dealing with. This isn’t a get-training-on-the-job. You can’t do that.”

At last week’s debate, Graham responded that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues.

Graham then touted her family’s service in the military, saying she’s “not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”

In an interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity the following evening, Graham acknowledged the fumble and leaned into attacks on her lack of experience, saying she’s since talked to voters and they appreciate her candor and that she’s not a “career politician.”

“I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan, but you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” she said. “I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

Trump echoed a similar defense when asked Friday about the gaffe, telling reporters that Graham “was being honest.”

“She’s surrounded by very good people, and she said that she’s totally for the military,” the president said.

As Graham has continued to brand herself as a political outsider, her opponent has repeatedly attacked her as the candidate backed by “the Washington elite,” pointing to her donors, which include Boeing’s political action committee, private equity firm Blackstone’s chief executive officer, social media platform TikTok’s head of public policy, and tech company Palantir’s head of defense chief of staff, according to South Carolina-based news outlet The State .

But Graham has pushed back on these efforts, saying earlier this month, according to The State, “When people give to me, that means they support me.”

“That doesn’t necessarily mean I support them,” she added.

The race has drawn millions of dollars from individual donors as well as from super PACs. In the last week of the race alone, Security is Strength PAC contributed more than $1.8 million and Palmetto Action gave nearly $1.2 million to boost Graham or oppose Norman, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records. Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a renewable energy-backed group, announced on Aug. 14 that it would spend $1 million to defeat Norman.

Norman’s funding from outside groups is dwarfed by Graham’s, but his campaign has benefited from his personal wealth. He donated $1.3 million to his own campaign on Aug. 17, four days after giving another $400,000, according to FEC reports.

Endorsements in the race have also swung more in Graham’s favor. On Monday alone, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) campaigned with the senator, and Trump joined a tele-rally with Graham at night for a last-ditch push to encourage South Carolinians to vote.

But last Friday, Norman got a boost when former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R), who came in fourth place during the special primary this month, backed Norman over Graham.

Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who came in a close third, backed Graham, who rallied in his district with Trump on Friday.

The results of the Aug. 11 primary were close, with Graham and Norman advancing with 32.75 percent and 24.62 percent, respectively, followed by Fry with 19.66 percent and Sanford with 14.94 percent.

Public polling has been limited in the couple of weeks since, and the dynamics have changed. As a result, many political observers are going in blind on Tuesday, waiting to see to what extent the debate, cash and Trump’s support will make a difference in the outcome.

“If you’re in the lead and … you have the support of the president, it’s a pretty good place to be,” Skelley said. “So I’m not necessarily saying that I think Graham is going to lose. I just think that this race really does feel up in the air.”

articles.title: Trump’s fight with GOP senators over trade intensifies
articles.summary: President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods. Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods .

Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50 percent tariffs on imports that could impact auto and housing prices has sparked a furious response from GOP senators across the party’s political spectrum.

“I think it’s a mistake. It’s what happens when he has advisers trying to micromanage things. They’re skating where the puck is versus where it needs to be. If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said at the Capitol Monday.

“Every time the government micromanages the economy, consumers suffer,” Tillis warned.

Tillis is one of several Republicans from an agriculture-heavy state to warn against allowing cheap beef imports to flood the U.S. market over the next three months — something that Trump hopes will bring down the price of an American diet staple through the midterm election.

Senate Republican Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), the second-ranking member of the Senate Republican leadership, declared Monday that “Americans want US beef on the table — not foreign imports.”

“Wyoming ranchers produce the highest quality beef in the world. Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier – not harder – for Wyoming ranchers to feed America,” he posted on X, the social media platform.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership, warned that opening U.S. markets to cheaper imports is “ill-advised” and will hurt domestic producers.

“Beef prices are too high for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small. Imported beef below market prices will only put more pressure on our cattlemen,” Cotton argued on social media.

“I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider. We need to support our cattlemen, grow the herd, and let the market work,” Cotton wrote.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also took to social media to dismiss Trump’s move as a “quick fix” and argued it’s out of step with the president’s efforts to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity with tariffs, such as those he’s threatening against Canada.

“What our market really needs is a stable, America-First national policy that promotes American beef rather than continuing to import foreign beef as a quick ‘fix.’ This instability harms hardworking American ranchers and consumers who want American-made beef,” he wrote.

“This is the exact opposite approach we take compared to manufacturing, and it doesn’t make sense,” Rounds added.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), a member of the Agriculture Committee, shared that relatively strong beef prices were a “bright spot” for the nation’s “struggling agriculture industry.”

“Importing beef below market prices will only put further downward pressure on the livestock sector, endangering what has been a bright spot in a struggling agriculture industry,” the Kansas senator wrote on social media. “I urge President Trump to halt this action, listen to ranchers and let the free markets work.”

Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa), Deb Fischer (Neb.) and Pete Ricketts (Neb.) also raised alarms over foreign beef showing up in American grocery stores.

Grassley said he was “concerned” while Fischer said she was “extremely disappointed by this decision” and Ricketts warned that “flooding the market with lower quality beef” would hurt Nebraska farmers and ranchers.

Yet Trump appears to be more sensitive to ground beef prices, which have risen by approximately 20 percent since he took office in January of 2025.

The average price of ground beef reached $6.89 per pound in July.

Trump pledged that imported beef will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices” over the next three months.

Some Democratic candidates, such as Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek who’s eyeing a Senate seat, are highlighting “skyrocketing” beef prices on the campaign trail.

But many Republicans don’t think that allowing cheap imports into the country is the best solution.

“Increasing beef imports would lead to more uncertainty and instability for our farmers,” said Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the GOP candidate in Iowa’s Senate race.

“We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers,” she wrote on social media.

The criticism from GOP senators of Trump’s decision to pause tariffs on beef imports comes as other Republican senators are pushing back against Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on an array of Canadian imports and his threat to impose equally high fees on even more.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race in a state that voted for former President Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last two presidential elections, called Trump’s threatened tariffs against Canada “a mistake.”

“We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products,” Collins told News Center Maine in an interview Monday.

Collins was one of four Republicans who voted last year to revoke Trump’s tariffs against Canada. She and Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Rand Paul (Ky.) and Mitch McConnell (Ky.) voted with Democrats to pass a resolution blocking them.

Six House Republicans voted with Democrats to pass a similar measure in the House last year.

Former Trump economic adviser Stephen Moore warned that any gains that domestic businesses might get from higher tariffs on Canadian goods are likely outweighed by the “pain” felt by U.S. consumers and businesses that import Canadian products or sell to Canadian markets.

“Probably the pain is not worth the gain. And you know, I’ve been a bit of a skeptic on the tariff front with respect to the Trump strategy,” Moore told Fox Business in an interview Monday.

He warned that raising the cost of Canadian goods may come while Americans are still coping with higher energy prices because of Iran war’s impact on oil and gas prices.

“We’re in a sticky situation obviously in Iran with respect to those negotiations. Now … do I think now is a good time to fight a trade war with Canada? Probably not,” he said. “Commodity prices are rising right now in the U.S. That’s a bad sign. That’s an indication that inflation continues to tick up.”

Tillis on Monday warned that charging steep tariffs on Canadian goods threatens to disrupt the economies of border states — such as Maine — that are closely integrated with the Canadian economy.

“Let the economy do what the economy’s doing. Get the trade relationships with Canada done versus all this volatility. You’re going to address more price fluctuations by doing this than all these gimmicks,” Tillis said.

The North Carolina senator warned that Republicans are running out of time to help farmers before the midterm elections as both a farm bill, which includes relief programs for ranchers hurt by drought and fire, and a budget reconciliation package, which includes $12 billion in emergency assistance to farmers, is stalled in the Senate.

“We’ve got 71 days” until the election “and right now we don’t have a positive message to tell farm country,” he said. “And we haven’t since Liberation Day last year, which is why I was concerned.”

Trump announced sweeping global tariffs on April 2, 2025, which the president proclaimed “Liberation Day.”

articles.title: The Memo: Trump and Bessent crank up economic pressure on Iran as other options fall short
articles.summary: Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the…
articles.body:
Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the globe.”

The hope within the administration seems to be that turning up the economic heat on Iran can produce tangible results without the baleful complications that could result from the two other broad options before the president.

If President Trump were to return to all-out war, he would risk a new spike in oil prices, Iranian reprisals aimed at U.S. allies in the Gulf, and a further diminution of American munition stockpiles. Even then, it is not clear that a definitive victory would be achieved without putting U.S. boots on Iranian soil — a scenario that has vanishingly thin support from the public.

If, on the other hand, Trump were to sue for peace right now, Iranian recalcitrance — and an apparent belief in Tehran that they retain plenty of leverage — would require him to make sizeable concessions.

The memorandum of understanding signed in June provided a preview of how such an approach would be received: Negatively.

The memorandum drew criticism from GOP hawks, who suggested it was too soft on Iran; from liberal opponents, who asked rhetorically what the war had been for in the first place; and from Israel, which jointly launched the war with the U.S. in late February.

So, on Monday it fell to Bessent to put some flesh on the bones of Trump’s earlier threats to up the economic pressure on Iran. The president, in a morning social media post, had insisted in his customary all-caps style that “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

The Treasury secretary communicates in a different register to his boss, but his language was aggressive all the same.

The administration’s objective, he said, was “to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Taking questions from reporters after his prepared remarks, Bessent characterized the U.S. as intent upon the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.

When it came to the U.S. desire to see other nations comply with Washington’s demands to cut off Iran or face secondary sanctions, Bessent warned, “We do not have infinite patience here.”

There were some definite lines of economic attack — but also a lot of detail that was not filled in.

For example, Bessent asserted that five areas of activity by which Iran sustains itself would be targeted: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also insisted that branches of Iran’s Bank Melli “must be shuttered and dark.”

Bessent also contended, even as he spoke, that an office within the Treasury Department was “sanctioning over 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that enable the Iranian regime to procure illicit nuclear and missile technology, conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.”

Yet, alongside the tough talk, there was also some vagueness.

Importantly, a sizeable question mark hangs over how aggressive the administration is prepared to be with China, which is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil exports.

Asked about that topic, Bessent asserted both that “no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” and that “the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy.”

It is, of course, rather debatable how committed the Trump administration is to quiet diplomacy. A few hours before Bessent’s appearance before the cameras, Trump had delivered a new jab in an unrelated trade dispute with the U.S.’s northern neighbor, beginning a lengthy social media post by declaring, “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years.”

That being so, Bessent’s supposed commitment to a softer, more private approach could also function to provide cover for ambivalence about how hard to push Beijing.

The unignorable backdrop to all the machinations is the unpopularity of the war with the American public.

Trump’s approval on Iran in the RealClearPolitics polling average is deep underwater. Roughly 61 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of the issue, while about 35 percent approve.

The war is intertwined with voters’ chief concern — rising prices and the cost of living. The average gas price nationally was roughly $4.10 per gallon on Monday, according to AAA , having been just below $3 before the war began.

Inflationary pressures, in part caused by the Iran war, are also part of the reason why there have been some jitters on the bond market recently. Bessent stepped in to try to calm the unease last week, with only partial success.

Put it all together, and it is an inhospitable landscape for Republicans seeking office in November’s midterms.

For now, the administration is clearly recalibrating its rhetoric.

Even the pugilistic Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on Monday that, although he was not “foreclosing” using direct strikes on Iran, “economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now .”

Bessent, in a lesser-noted part of his Monday remarks, characterized the U.S. armed forces as having “laid the groundwork” for the achievement of American objectives.

This was a notably more circumspect assessment than those given by other senior administration officials in the early part of the war.

So, for now, the Iranian economy is the battlefield.

The big question is how fast, if at all, the U.S. can secure a meaningful victory.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: South Carolina runoff pits America First against MAGA
articles.summary: Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas. But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of…
articles.body:
Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas.

But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of President Trump’s Iran war strategy with Republican voters.

Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) already-legendary line — “I’m not that informed on national security” — is thought by many to have recast what had appeared to be a perfunctory runoff with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) into a competitive race. I say perfunctory because in the first round, the MAGA candidates got most of the vote, almost all of which presumably would filter down to Graham in today’s contest.

There were five candidates who got at least 5 percent of the vote in the first round of the snap primary on Aug. 11, held to replace Graham’s brother, Lindsey. The elder Graham died in July after winning renomination for a fifth Senate term, leaving the state GOP without a Senate candidate in a good Democratic year — one in which the blue team happens to have a nonterrible Senate nominee in Annie Andrews. It’s South Carolina, where no Democratic Senate candidate has come within even 10 points of winning in decades. But still, a bad enough Republican nominee in a bad enough year could have put the Palmetto State race on the map, at least notionally.

There’s plenty that’s weird and wild in South Carolina Republican politics, so Gov. Henry McMaster (R) took no chances and appointed Darline Graham to serve out the final months of her brother’s term. That appointment and her decision to seek a full, six-year term came at the behest of Trump, who has had his own troubles with South Carolina politics.

Before Lindsey Graham became Trump’s wingman and shadow secretary of State, he had been among Trump’s fiercest early critics. And then there’s former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R), who went the other direction, serving deferentially as Trump’s first-term ambassador to the United Nations before running a dogged if doomed race against Trump as he sought renomination in 2024. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) also opposed Trump that year, but only halfheartedly and not for very long.

Knowing that South Carolina can be problematic and looking for another member of the Senate MAGA caucus, Trump clearly judged that backing a sentimental favorite in the beloved sister of the late senator would be easy electoral politics and give him an easy vote in Washington, where things have only been getting harder for the lame-duck commander in chief.

In that way, Graham’s gaffe was proof of concept for Trump. Asked about her professed ignorance ahead of his trip to campaign for Graham, Trump told reporters , “She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants. She understands that national security is my thing.” That presumably applies when his “thing” is increasingly unpopular with voters.

Trump’s electoral assumption about Graham was proven right in Round 1 of the snap primary, when she got about a third of the vote, besting Norman by 8 points. Norman is not MAGA but rather a dissident from South Carolina’s underlying don’t-tread-on-me tradition. The House Freedom Caucus is pretty much a MAGA operation now, but back when Norman joined in 2017, there was still a little of the rebellious streak left. Norman has always had a little of Marjorie Taylor Greene energy about him — more about the movement than the man. But he’s also won friends among traditional conservatives for his hawkishness on spending and Reaganite foreign policy. It wasn’t just home-state sentiment that led Norman to back Haley in 2024 or Haley to back him now.

In third place on Aug. 11 was Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who is stone-cold MAGA to his core. Team Trump backed Fry in his 2022 primary bid against then-Rep. Tom Rice (R-S.C.), an old-school conservative who had voted to impeach Trump for trying to overturn the 2020 election. Fry beat Rice in a major show of strength for Trump early in his interregnum, making Fry a made man in MAGA. He got nearly 20 percent of the vote in Round 1 and then, to the surprise of no one, fell in behind Trump-endorsed Graham for the runoff.

Next in the running was Mark Sanford, the former governor and congressman who was a conservative heartthrob until the vivid unraveling of his marriage while still the state’s chief executive. Sanford is neither MAGA nor America First in any strict sense. He’s a traditional, small-government conservative with some areas of overlap with both groups but is clearly and stubbornly a dissident. He is also a hated figure in MAGA World for his frequent opposition to Trump during Sanford’s House tenure. No surprise, then, that he is backing Norman over Graham on Tuesday. It’s an echo of the onetime conservative dream team in the state that once included Sanford, Haley, Scott and former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.), now long eclipsed by Trump and McMaster’s very effective machine.

Rounding out the top five was Mark Lynch, who has a massive appliance store in South Carolina’s Upstate. Lynch proved that he is more America First than MAGA when he ran against Lindsey Graham in the original June primary. While Lynch is part of a movement that takes out-there stances on things like allegations of election corruption and vaccines , he is willing to publicly disagree with Trump. And given that his central charge against the elder Graham was that he was too much of an internationalist, one suspects Lynch isn’t a “forever war” kind of guy. He too has endorsed Norman .

All of which makes the Iran question particularly interesting. Darline Graham accidentally summed up the MAGA Iran position: Back the president and let him do his “thing.” The America First position tends to be that the war was a betrayal of Trump’s promises and a mistake from the start that is only getting worse. The conservative stance seems to be that bombing Iran could have been the right move but that Trump has subsequently blundered it away. The candidates in this race have been cagy about their own stances, but voters are going to make their own inferences.

Not everyone who voted in Round 1 will vote in Round 2, but we can use the results as a rough guide for where today’s electorate started. The MAGA candidates — Graham and Fry — combined for 52 percent of the vote. America Firsters and conservatives — Norman, Sanford and Lynch — combined for 46 percent, with 2 percent sprinkled across minor candidates.

The question today is whether Graham’s textbook Kinsley gaffe is worth at least 4 points for Norman with swing among voters who are having their own doubts about whether the president should be running foreign policy without supervision. Norman’s hope has got to be that he’s got enough cred with both America First and the conservatives to make it happen.

Stirewalt is the politics editor for The Hill, veteran campaign and elections journalist and best-selling author of books about American political history.

articles.title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
articles.body:
In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting "tariffs and war".

If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate.

"When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas," Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. "That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I'm a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn't have got in the race if I didn't."

The founder of the largest Methodist denomination in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party's primary, though Marshall is still favored to win.

For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress's upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they've named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so.

The US president's slumping approval ratings and the Iran war's impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats' chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin.

This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a "blue wave" of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win.

Asked what he thought of Schumer's prediction, Hamilton said: "I don't agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I'm telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don't care what else happens across the country."

No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber's Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since.

Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor's mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state.

"Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there's something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won't pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor," said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka.

But Hamilton's experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for "a very competitive race" against Marshall. "What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He's been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years," he said.

Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump's debunked claims of fraud in that year's presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration's funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment.

Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. He mulled running as an independent, but ultimately filed as a Democrat, saying he was concerned that he'd split the vote if he wasn't in a party and agreed with its views on "healthcare, education [and] social safety nets".

"Those are things that matter a lot to me, and my faith leads in that direction," he said.

A self-described "moderate or independent-minded Democrat", his campaign recently released an ad where Hamilton likens Kansas's position in the middle of the country to his own approach to the politics that would await him in Washington DC.

Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being "a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas", and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he'd put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m.

The senator recently called his opponent a "megachurch pastor that's too woke for Kansas", the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context.

Like so much in his career, Hamilton's chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as "a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas" and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran.

"The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas," Slattery said. "It's the bottom line."

articles.title: Smithsonian-linked museum in El-Sayed’s backyard puts America’s post-9/11 response on trial
articles.summary: A Smithsonian Institution affiliate in Dearborn features exhibits arguing Arabs suffered unfair treatment after the Sept. 11 attacks on America.
articles.body: DEARBORN, MI – Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a Smithsonian affiliate in Michigan continues to use its 9/11 exhibits and anniversary programming to focus on discrimination and government actions in the attacks' aftermath, while giving less attention to the nearly 3,000 people killed that day, Fox News Digital found. The Arab American National Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, features an exhibit arguing that Arab Americans "suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th," both from the attacks themselves and from what the museum describes as unfair treatment by the U.S. government afterward. Since its founding, the museum has repeatedly hosted programs examining what it describes as discriminatory consequences of the U.S. response to 9/11. Fox News Digital visited the museum earlier this month, reviewed its exhibits and gift shop, and examined years of anniversary programming and federal funding records. The AANM has received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and is also an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. The Smithsonian has been under intense scrutiny from conservative lawmakers in recent months for allegedly allowing political bias to influence its presentation of history. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED One placard criticizes the government’s post-9/11 detention of immigrants investigated for possible terrorist links, noting that "virtually none were charged" in connection with terrorism. "The Arab American community suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th. As with all Americans, they suffered the horror and grief. However, Arab Americans were unfairly held responsible, yet not a single Arab American was found guilty of any connection to September 11th," it reads. On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center, and one into the Pentagon. Passengers and crew fought back aboard United Flight 93, the fourth plane, prompting the hijackers to crash the plane in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the largest investigation in FBI history. The museum placard also argues that Arabs faced harsher immigration enforcement after the attacks, saying some were "deported for minor visa violations or petty offenses which previously would have been overlooked." HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE' In the 11 months after the attacks, immigration authorities detained 762 noncitizens on immigration charges in connection with the FBI’s terrorism investigation, including for overstaying visas or entering the country illegally, according to a Justice Department inspector general report. The watchdog found that some detainees with no terrorism ties were treated harshly and held under unnecessarily restrictive conditions. Public opinion also showed a more complicated picture of the post-9/11 backlash. President George W. Bush publicly urged Americans not to blame Muslims for the attacks, and polling later suggested attitudes toward Muslim Americans actually improved in the immediate aftermath. The share of Americans who viewed Muslim Americans favorably rose from 45% in March 2001 to 59% in November, two months after the attacks, according to the Pew Research Center. Beyond its permanent exhibit, AANM has repeatedly used programming around the 9/11 anniversary to examine discrimination and law-enforcement policies affecting Arab and Muslim communities. The museum holds a "solidarity" town hall each year, where criticism of the American reaction to 9/11 is often the focus. The online description of the event does not mention the deaths connected to the attacks themselves, but rather "offers a safe space for communities to reflect and engage in dialogue about the harmful prejudices that Arab and Muslim (and anyone perceived to be Arab or Muslim) individuals face on both an individual and systemic level." One such town hall in 2018 examined "how communities of color have been targeted through the frame of national security and profiled as violent threats." A year later, the AANM’s annual town, which received support from the National Endowment for the Arts, criticized how "institutions and communities of color have been infiltrated" by law enforcement as well as how leaders of those groups have been "targeted" following 9/11. SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES The AANM was founded in 2005, partially in response to the increased scrutiny directed at the Arab American community following the attack on the World Trade Center. In addition to receiving well over half a million dollars in funding from the NEH over its lifetime to support its exhibits and educational programming, the museum also benefited from a $385,000 grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development which helped it expand its physical footprint in 2013. It received further HUD funding, over half a million dollars, between 2017 and 2019 as well as at least $50,000 from the State Department between 2016 and 2017, according to annual reports published by the museum. Dearborn, where about 54.5% of residents are of Middle Eastern or North African descent, is a key political center in Michigan ahead of one of the country’s most competitive Senate races this year. Socialist-aligned Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the Senate, drew strong support from the city earlier this month. The museum’s focus extends beyond its criticism of the U.S. response to 9/11. On Sept. 10 — the eve of the 25th anniversary of the attacks — the AANM is scheduled to host a screening of "Seeds for Liberation," a film that portrays Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack as part of a decades-long Palestinian "struggle" and places it within a broader history of "anti-imperialist and decolonial movements." During Fox News Digital’s visit earlier this month, a section of the museum was dedicated to art criticizing Israel's alleged "occupation" of Palestinian land. One piece of art, the word "wall" presented in a stylized print, accuses the Israeli government of perpetuating a system of "apartheid." The art installation broadly accuses Israel of targeting civilians in military operations, denying basic necessities to Palestinians and unjustly occupying land. FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM One placard accompanying a sculpture states that Israel has killed more than 2,000 Palestinian children since Sept. 29, 2000, citing If Americans Knew (IAK). The placard’s sourcing is itself controversial. Some pro-Palestinian organizations have distanced themselves from IAK over allegations of antisemitism and ties to white supremacists, allegations the group has disputed. IAK also operates a news site that has published articles rejecting the designation of Hamas as a terrorist organization. Another placard attached to a sculpture pulls a quote from Defense of Children International Palestine, which the Israeli government designated as a terrorist organization in 2021. DCIP and human rights groups have disputed the designation. The museum gift shop also sells Palestinian-themed merchandise, including map-shaped magnets and key chains, coloring books promising to help children "explore Palestinian heritage" and keffiyehs. IN CHARTS: A VISUAL BREAKDOWN OF THE SMITHSONIAN'S BILLION-DOLLAR TAXPAYER-FUNDED BUDGET CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The AANM, Smithsonian, NEA and NEH did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Friday. Smithsonian affiliates, like the AANM, are independently operated museums that maintain formal partnerships with the Smithsonian, providing them with access to artifact loans, educational resources and consultations from institutional experts. In recent months, the Smithsonian has faced mounting pressure from Republican lawmakers and the president over allegations that its museums advance left-of-center ideological causes through their exhibits. Officials have threatened funding cuts against the institution if it does not root out what the Trump administration characterizes as anti-American bias.

articles.title: Florida, hard-hit by Obamacare drop-off, feels the squeeze of rising healthcare costs
articles.summary: Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.  After Republicans in Congress let en...
articles.body:
ST. CLOUD, Fla. (AP) — Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.

It was his worst kitchen accident to date. But having given up his Affordable Care Act health insurance plan in January because of a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford, the 21-year-old in St. Cloud didn't have the money for emergency care.

"Going to the hospital for it wasn't even an option," he said, gesturing toward his finger before preparing a pot roast for his aunt and uncle in their suburban home. "My first thought was, 'how am I going to fix this?'"

After Republicans in Congress let enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans expire in January, millions of Americans including Button had to decide whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost — or risk going without it.

Months later, with no action from lawmakers to replace the lost funds, they're facing the consequences. Some are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost.

Florida, whose large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, has become one of the nation's most visible epicenters of that impact.

Figures first reported by The Associated Press showed that about 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act plans this year — more than in any other state . Thousands more who kept coverage are struggling to get by, as prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes .

While Florida had the most affected residents, its struggles are reflective of broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them.

In the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans, the cost of healthcare is a major campaign issue. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies.

Button, who is estranged from his parents, asked his uncle for help with his bloodied finger. With a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings, it healed. But the scar still gnaws at Button as a symbol of what else could go wrong.

"It just feels like I'm living in a house of cards," he said.

Florida's population and politics make it ground zero for ACA fallout

Last fall, debate over the expiring subsidies consumed Congress, resulting in a record 43-day government shutdown as Democrats insisted on extending the COVID-era assistance and most Republicans refused.

Fast forward almost a year and lawmakers rarely reference the topic anymore. The administration says it is addressing affordability with fraud-busting efforts and deals with drug companies, but Congress hasn't passed any significant legislation to lower health costs.

In part due to its large number of construction, hospitality and small business workers — and also because its Republican-led legislature never expanded the Medicaid safety-net health program — Florida has the largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the country. At just over 3.8 million enrollees, it represents about a fifth of the nation's total enrolled population.

Of the roughly 443,000 Floridians who left the marketplace, most are likely going without insurance, according to Cynthia Cox, a vice president at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. She said that's because it is typically a "place of last resort" to get coverage.

The data doesn't tell the stories of those who kept insurance. Tracy Rand, a licensed mental health counselor in Leesburg, Florida, is one of them.

Ever since getting her ovaries removed last year due to benign but painful tumors, she has had severe menopause symptoms that require medication, including an overactive bladder and hot flashes that cause piercing headaches.

She uses clear plastic containers to organize the more than 30 medicines and supplements she takes daily, their bottles crammed into a living-room drawer and a tray on her kitchen counter.

The 51-year-old's Affordable Care Act plan was going to surge in price this year from $55 a month to $1,100 a month, so she downgraded. Her new plan, with higher deductibles and copays, costs $160 a month.

To make that work in her budget, Rand quit a doctoral program she was working toward, started buying groceries at cheaper stores, gave up once-monthly dinners out with her husband and stopped meeting friends regularly at a paint-your-own pottery studio.

It's been a difficult adjustment, but a necessary one for her health.

Rand said the prospect of insurers raising rates again fills her with dread.

"I don't know what else we can get rid of," she said, covering her face with her hands. "I don't know if we're going to have to file bankruptcy.″

Clinics for the uninsured are a saving grace — but they can't take everyone

In Orlando's leafy, brick-paved neighborhood of Colonialtown South, Tarsha Watson found her lifeline. A clinic there called Grace Medical Home provides low-income, uninsured Floridians with comprehensive care for a $5 per-visit fee.

Watson, 54, has a master's degree in business administration, but she hasn't been able to find work since losing her job two years ago. That means she doesn't have health insurance. When she explored Affordable Care Act coverage, she was quoted $600 per month, far out of her reach.

At Grace, Watson learned her blood sugar is high and that she needed to lose weight. Now, she walks laps around her backyard pool and does Tai Chi YouTube tutorials to focus on fitness. She said she wishes everyone could have her experience.

"It's very hard out here," she said. "It's not enough."

At the clinic, patients cycle in and out of a wide hallway lined with appointment rooms as doctors scan supply shelves for complimentary over-the-counter medications. The expansive building has separate areas for dental, mental health, vision and pediatric care.

CEO Stephanie Garris said it's one of 110 free or charitable clinics in Florida, but that's not enough to handle demand. To treat more people in response to the Affordable Care Act changes, it recently started hosting a mobile acute care clinic for walk-in patients.

Garris said Grace Medical Home treated about 1,350 people last year. Every year, they take about 350 new patients.

"Would I love to double that, triple that? Of course," Garris said. "I just think in the reality, with the huge number of uninsured that we have, it's just not possible."

Health costs become an issue in midterm campaigns

For U.S. Rep. Darren Soto, a Democrat defending his seat in a sprawling — and now much redder — redrawn district south of Orlando, health costs are a campaign focal point.

He said his district, which is near various theme parks, had the second-largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the nation, in part because many small tourism businesses can't offer employees health insurance.

"I just hear it everywhere I go," he said. His Republican opponent, Navy veteran and former Trump administration official Dan Green, did not answer emailed questions about the subsidies but has emphasized affordability of groceries and property insurance as campaign priorities.

Soto voted with Democrats and some Republicans — including a few from Florida — to save the subsidies last year. The Republican majority declined and suggested other ideas, including funding Americans' health savings accounts. No law along those lines has passed yet.

Button, a Democrat in Soto's district, said he is open to different reforms for health costs, but said politicians aren't acting fast enough.

"They keep trying to make excuse after excuse," he said. "I don't have six months to a year to wait for you guys to pass this through the hoops that you need to."

articles.title: Trump says US considering renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's remarks come amid a deepening cross-border trade feud that has increasingly centered on Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
articles.body:
Minister of Industry of Canada, Mélanie Joly, has responded to President Donald Trump's comments that the United States is giving "serious consideration" to renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," Joly told reporters on Tuesday when asked about Trump's statement, the latest escalation in his increasingly bitter dispute with Canada as trade talks between the two countries remain stalled. "We're proud of the Great Lakes… and we'll stand up for what we have," she said. "I really think that, with all these shenanigans happening. We'll just be smart and we'll be strategic, and we'll fight back."

In a Tuesday post on Truth Social, Trump had suggested the move was under consideration because the U.S. did not expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer." The president later shared on his social-media platform a map of the lake with its current name crossed out and replaced with "Lake America." The proposal lands as relations between Washington and Ottawa are under fresh strain following the breakdown of trade talks and months of sparring between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"It is quite possible that Canadians could see the appropriation of Lake Ontario and its renaming as part of the larger effort on the part of the U.S. to exert its influence territorially," Derek Alderman, a cultural and historical geographer, told Newsweek . He added that the move seemed intended "to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada."

Meanwhile, Reuben Rose-Redwood, Professor of Geography at the University of Victoria, called it "pure rage bait" and a "well-worn move from the Trump playbook akin to calling Canada the '51st State' or renaming the Gulf of Mexico to capture media attention."

"Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario is pure rage bait aimed at stoking anger among Canadians while distracting Americans from the fact that Trump overplayed his hand in the trade negotiations with Canada," he told Newsweek .

The official White House X account later shared a map of the United States, in the style of Lego, which labelled the lake which borders New York as "Lake America."

However, it appears that the map is incorrect with D.C. labeled as being located in North Carolina in the White House's map.

"How much drinking water did you idiots use up just to put DC and NJ in the wrong places?" The Lincoln Project asked in response to the post on X, referring to the assumption that the map was created via AI.

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr — CSPAN (@cspan) August 25, 2026

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr

Newsweek has contacted Ford's office and the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for comment.

The White House referred Newsweek to Trump's Truth Social post when approached for clarification on his proposal.

The president's remarks come following the breakdown of trade talks between U.S. and Canadian negotiators on Friday.

Carney said last-minute changes by the American side were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the breakdown and told CNBC's Squawk Box that Ottawa's negotiators sought their own 11th-hour additions.

The U.S. has now imposed 50 percent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products —targeting certain motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages, and dairy, as well as a host of other goods together worth around $20 billion—and Trump has threatened the same duties on Canadian cars, automotive parts and steel.

Prime Minister Carney has said the country will match these "dollar for dollar," and Ottawa is preparing to announce a specific set of countermeasures as soon as Tuesday which will come into effect in September.

Ford has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the administration's Canada policies. Ford has previously threatened trade retaliation and restriction s affecting exports to the U.S., making Ontario a frequent focus of Trump's criticism as tensions between the neighboring countries intensify.

Ford has said that his country was prepared for "an economic war." He told the Associated Press that "everything was on the table" when it came to responding to the new tariffs, including limiting restricting electricity exports and critical mineral supplies from Ontario.

Ford made a similar threat early last year, shortly after Trump's return to office and following the announcement of tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.

The cross-border trade feud between the historic allies has often centered on Ford, who on Monday called Trump a dictator and said during a news conference in Hamilton that the U.S. president could "kiss my a**."

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq — The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, sitting on the U.S.-Canada border between Ontario and New York. It is the smallest Great Lake by surface area but serves as a key shipping link between the Great Lakes region and the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Major cities on its shores include Toronto, Hamilton and Rochester.

The city derives its name from the lake, which got it from an indigenous word predating both Canada and the United States. It is usually traced to the Wyandot (Huron) word Ontarí'io or a related Iroquoian term, variously translated as "great" or "beautiful" water.

Rose-Redwood said that while the Trump administration can order the name to be changed on U.S. federal maps, it has no power over whether Canada or international map makers do so. The last time Trump announced he was altering the name of a location, the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, other countries failed to follow suit.

"Trump can certainly instruct the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to rename Lake Ontario on U.S. federal maps, yet Canadian and international mapmakers are not obliged to comply with any decrees coming from the White House," Rose-Redwood told Newsweek .

"Although President Trump's threat of a name change is meant to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada that has ensued, it actually could backfire by further alienating the Canadian people," said Alderman, a former president of the American Association of Geographers. "Place names are quite important to people's identity as well as key resources in educating our youth and being key parts of treaties, policy documents and maps used for a variety of economic and political activities."

Alderman, now a professor in the University of Tennessee's Geography & Sustainability Department, told Newsweek that such a change would only exacerbate fears that Trump is hoping to turn the country into a "51st state," while also threatening Canadian identity.

"On a deeper level, the president's abrupt and unilateral threat to rename Lake Ontario, seemingly without proper public discussion or governmental deliberation, would say something negative about how the names on our maps, landscapes and bodies of water are being reduced to pawns and weapons in the latest battles over trade negotiation and insults traded between U.S. and Canadian leaders," he added.

The proposal would also create an unexpected classroom headache. Generations of students have memorized the Great Lakes using the acronym "HOMES" for Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior. A different name for Lake Ontario would render the mnemonic obsolete.

The name Lake Ontario predates both the United States and Canada and has Indigenous origins.

The name is generally traced to an Iroquoian term, often rendered as Ontarí'io or Ontario , which has been interpreted as meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water." The precise linguistic origin and meaning have been debated, but the name was in use long before European settlement and eventually became the name used for the lake and the province of Ontario.

That history gives the proposed name change an additional cultural dimension. Lake Ontario is not simply a label on a modern map: its name is connected to Indigenous languages and centuries of history in the Great Lakes region.

The lake's name was subsequently adopted by the province of Ontario, which was established as a British North American province in 1867 and later became Canada's most populous province.

A move by the U.S. to refer to the lake as "Lake America" on federal maps would therefore place a modern political label over a name with a much longer history.

Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, but it is considerably deeper than its size might suggest.

The lake has an average depth of approximately 283 feet and reaches a maximum depth of about 802 feet. It covers roughly 7,340 square miles with about one-quarter of its surface area in the United States and the remainder in Canada.

Lake Ontario is also an important part of the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence waterway. Water from the other Great Lakes flows through Lake Ontario before continuing down the St. Lawrence River toward the Atlantic Ocean.

Its shores include major population centers including Toronto, Hamilton and Kingston in Ontario, as well as Rochester and Oswego in New York.

The lake's geography also underscores why a change to its name would have consequences beyond a map label. Lake Ontario is a major international waterway, forming part of the border between two countries and supporting shipping, tourism, fishing, industry and millions of people living around its shores.

List of Places Trump Has Renamed Since Returning to Office

Trump's suggestion that Lake Ontario could become "Lake America" would be the latest example of his efforts to rename or rebrand prominent geographic features since returning to office. In 2025, he ordered federal agencies to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in place of the Gulf of Mexico and restored Mount McKinley as the federal name for Alaska's Denali, reversing a 2015 Obama-era change.

The president has also shown a willingness to use provocative place-naming proposals as a political statement. Earlier this month, he shared an image on Truth Social depicting the Strait of Hormuz as "NEW U.S. Territory" and publicly entertained the idea of asserting U.S. control over the strategically important waterway.

While it remains unclear whether any formal effort will be made to rename Lake Ontario, the proposal fits a broader pattern of Trump using symbolic geographic branding to advance political messages, particularly in disputes involving trade, national identity and U.S. influence abroad.

articles.title: Bessent slow rolls ‘Economic D-Day’ on Iran
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Voters head to polls in GOP runoffs ▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now ▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs ▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of…
articles.body:
▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now

▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs

▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of a threat than immediately bringing the hammer down, at least for now.

Bessent issued a warning during a press conference for all countries to cut off business and other financial ties with Iran or else face significant sanctions.

The plan has been named “Operation Economic Outcast” and promoted as comparable to the U.S. invasion of Normandy during World War II. But Bessent avoided naming specific countries that the U.S. is seeking to pressure and didn’t share many specific actions or a timeline that the federal government would take.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said, when asked at a press conference why sanctions wouldn’t take effect immediately.

Bessent said diplomacy is happening behind the scenes, as President Trump is calling world leaders to get them to cut off Iran. He said officials from the State, Treasury and Defense departments are also calling their counterparts around the world.

He expressed confidence about the plan, saying that the U.S. has “already seen some results” and emphasizing that Trump can be “quite persuasive.”

But the announcement fell short of quite the boisterous threats that the president has been making for days leading up to the move, as he seeks to force Iran back to the bargaining table and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

Trump said any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline” to Iran will face “TREMENDOUS” economic consequences.

While the president hasn’t ruled out additional military action against Iran, he has shifted his focus to the economic realm amid growing warnings over depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles.

One complicating factor to the “outcast” plan is the role of China, which is Iran’s largest trading partner. Bessent said “no country is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” when asked plans for China.

Experts told NBC News that the success of Bessent’s announcement will depend on whether Iran’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — deem the U.S. threats credible.

Bessent also announced other actions designed to squeeze Iran economically, including placing sanctions on 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Treasury Department said it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating specific sectors of the Iranian economy, including digital assets, technology, aviation and shipping.

Iran’s currency, the rial, continued to take a hit on Monday, falling to a record low of about 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. U.S. markets seemed to mostly shrug at the news, as the Dow Jones finished slightly up compared to the start of the day, while Nasdaq and the S&P 500 finished slightly lower.

Signs of Iran’s economic struggles amid the war continue to multiply. The International Monetary Fund said its economy will contract by 5.4 percent this year, while the government is signaling a coming hike to fuel prices in a bid to buoy the economy, a move that will compound rising prices.

What’s less certain is whether that pain is increasing pressure on the hardline regime to end the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , who has led negotiations with the U.S., have pointed to the economic anxiety in remarks about the country’s war posture in recent days.

However, leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps are seen as digging in, promoting a more assertive approach to the war focused on “offensive operations.”

An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the “strategy of shifting the war to an offensive posture if Iran’s conditions are not met will undoubtedly transform the balance of power in the world,” CNN reported.

How much Iran’s military is willing to test that theory, or whether the U.S. is willing to put the screws to global powers still supporting Iran, are key questions in a war that has now gone on for almost six months.

Republican California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton revealed to NewsNation his plan to try to stop parents and teachers from having to pick up the cost of school supplies. It’s another way to address the affordability issue . As we saw last week, Trump had his own idea regarding importing beef to lower prices for consumers. However, American ranchers have panned the plan. So did Hilton when I spoke with him on Monday.

“I’m not a fan of that policy at all. I’ve been with our ranchers across the state, and they are really struggling,” Hilton told me . He also pointed the finger at Democrats. “The struggle in California is because of California policies, the regulations that they have to comply with, way more onerous than other states,” he added.

Bringing down prices in any form remains a key issue for Republicans, whether it be in the meat section, or school supplies section, of your local grocery store.

By the way, we are bringing back our Viewer’s Voice segment on Wednesday. Have a question for Congress? Email me at viewersvoice@newsnationnow.com . We’ll put your questions to Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.).
