The federal government is reportedly planning to revoke the visas for up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S. If the move goes through, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history.

The Trump administration formally removed Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list , a significant milestone for the country as its government under Ahmad al-Sharaa seeks to restore ties with the international community. The move will allow Damascus to fully rejoin the global financial system.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) assured the public that no one in the president’s circle would “get a pass” if Democrats win back control of the House in November. His comments came in response to some backlash to his reported meeting with Jared Kushner to discuss areas of common ground with the administration.

President Trump watches Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) speak at her campaign event at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C., Aug. 21, 2026. (Mic Smith, Associated Press)

RUNOFFS : Tonight’s primaries will provide two of the final major tests of Trump’s endorsement power in this year’s midterm primaries.

Trump has weighed into today’s GOP primary runoffs for South Carolina’s Senate seat and for Oklahoma’s governorship, expending political capital in two races that are anyone’s to win.

In South Carolina, Trump has thrown his weight behind Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who is serving out the final months of her late brother’s term as she seeks a full six-year term of her own. She faces Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a longtime member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus who is leaning on his experience in office.

Graham and Norman advanced to a runoff after earning about 33 percent and 25 percent, respectively, in the Aug. 11 special primary, setting off a two-week sprint to today’s runoff.

But without much public polling — and after Graham’s fumble over a national security question during last week’s debate — the race is up for grabs. One poll released late Monday night showed the race essentially tied .

Over in Oklahoma , Trump’s pick, Republican Mike Mazzei , finished less than a percentage point behind his opponent, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R), who was viewed as an early favorite in the race before Trump weighed in just two weeks before the June primary.

Drummond has faced the president’s ire over his resistance to a Trump-backed project to bring what would be the country’s largest aluminum smelter to his state and filed a suit to block the plant, arguing it would hurt residents and their land. Trump has also suggested Drummond was not supportive enough during his impeachment trials.

The president joined back-to-back tele-rallies last night with each candidate as he urged voters to turn out to the polls.

SCOTUS SURPRISE : The Supreme Court has lifted a federal judge’s block on Trump’s executive order implementing requirements for mail-in voting, with the majority finding that a handful of Democratic-leaning state sued too early for courts to weigh in.

The conservative majority ruled over the dissents of the court’s three liberals that the judge didn’t have the authority to block the order before the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) implements the new standards.

The ruling allows the president to move closer to instituting his order ahead of the midterms. Trump signed the order in March to direct his administration to create a list of verified citizens who are eligible to vote and for USPS to only send ballots to citizens on a state’s approved mail-in ballot list.

California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington co-led the lawsuit challenging the order, leading a total of nearly two dozen states and Washington, D.C.

The ruling covers the timing of the case but not the merits. Additional legal challenges may be to come, leaving whether the order can be implemented in time for November uncertain.

NEXT ROUND : Trump is already looking ahead to implementing another wave of steep tariffs on Canada following Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s announcement that his government will impose retaliatory tariffs against the U.S.

The president threatened Monday that he would place additional 50 percent tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting Jan. 1. That would be on top of the 50 percent tariffs that went into effect at the end of last week on a range of Canadian goods, including wine, furniture and cement.

Carney’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods — including dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment and electronics — will take effect Sept. 8.

Trade talks between the countries collapsed at the end of last week. Carney has said the U.S.’s terms were unacceptable, including a late demand that restrictions be placed on Canada’s ability to reach trade deals with other countries.

Trump administration officials have accused Canada of being the one making last-minute changes, with the president saying on Truth Social on Monday that Canada has been “ripping off” the U.S. for years.

TRY TRY AGAIN :The Trump administration is again planning to charge employers more than $100,000 for skilled international workers they hire through the H-1B work visa program, according to a notice of proposed rulemaking issued Monday by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

A federal judge in June struck down the Trump administration’s proposal for a $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications, ruling only Congress could levy taxes and set immigration laws.

But DHS’s proposed rule indicates that the fee would function as a “dedicated revenue mechanism” to recover some of the cost of administering the immigration system.

“The proposed H ‑ 1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a release.

INTRAPARTY BEEF : Senate Republicans are breaking with the president over his plan to pause tariffs on beef imports as he escalates duties on key Canadian products.

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports several Republicans from agriculture-heavy states are urging Trump against the plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quote tariffs.

Trump decided to use the pause to address consumers’ worries about rising food costs, but the Republicans said they’re concerned about cheap beef imports flooding the market in the coming months.

“They’re skating where the puck is versus where it needs to be. If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) brushed off Trump’s move as a “quick fix,” while Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), a member of the Agriculture Committee, said the relatively strong beef prices are a “bright spot” for a “struggling” agricultural industry.

Bolton reports Trump seems to be sensitive to ground beef costs, which have risen about 20 percent since he took office last January. Some Democratic candidates, including Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek , are emphasizing “skyrocketing” beef prices while campaigning.

Trump has vowed that imported beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices over the next three months. But many Republicans said allowing cheap imports isn’t the best solution.

WATER FIGHT: Nevada is suing the federal government over its finalized plan to force certain states to reduce their Colorado River water usage over the next 10 years, saying the cuts are too steep and could threaten people’s health and safety and devastate local economies.

“This isn’t about political posturing; this is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy,” Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) said in a statement.

The Colorado River provides water for agricultural, municipal and industrial uses for seven states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming.

The river has been facing a major drought and, as the climate gets drier, the states have had to negotiate the river’s future management, especially since the interim guidelines expire at the end of the year.

But, after the states failed to reach an agreement, the federal government had to step in, and last month, the Interior Department released a 10-year framework that would force California, Arizona and Nevada to cut up to 3 million acre-feet per year.

The three states recoiled at the proposal, and the Interior Department responded with a short-term plan that would instead require the three states to reduce their water use by 1.25 million acre-feet per year in 2027 and 2028.

But the department on Friday also finalized the 10-year plan, which the Trump administration has said is meant to be a flexible framework that is responsive to whatever the water conditions may be in the future.

And finally … Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas thanked Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) for standing up for him in the face of ethics complaints in recent years when the judge appeared on an episode of Cruz’s podcast released Monday.

“You’re one of the people who actually stands up, particularly at times when others seem to wither, and I appreciate it,” Thomas said on the episode of “Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

Thomas has faced scrutiny in recent years over allegations that he failed to disclose gifts, luxury travel and property transactions involving billionaire Harlan Crow , a GOP megadonor. He’s also faced criticism over perceived conflicts of interest given political activism from his wife, Ginni Thomas .

“That is very kind of you, and especially for you to observe that I stand up in the face of criticism and attacks, that is powerful coming from you because you’re someone who knows what that’s like and has done so in a way that has been world-changing,” Cruz responded.

articles.title: The victory lap on Trump’s nuclear campus plan is premature
articles.summary: Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan should clear five tests.
articles.body:
In late July, the Department of Energy announced that five states — Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho — had agreed to explore hosting Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses .

Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the campuses “massive generators of economic growth” that would be “crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance.” The American Nuclear Society echoed him, its president promising “multigenerational job creation, sustained economic growth, and new investment in education and workforce development.”

By folding nuclear waste into a sweeping economic development package, the department has invited states to compete for campuses that could co-locate multiple stages of the nuclear fuel cycle — such as uranium enrichment, fuel fabrication, spent fuel reprocessing, waste disposition and, in some states, advanced reactors. This is all while using the appeal of nuclear power investment to soften the politics of hosting long-term waste facilities.

It is an appealing vision. But five signed memoranda are not five host communities. No final host agreement has been signed, no construction funds awarded and the states have agreed only to continue negotiations. That is a real beginning, but it is not a victory. Treating it as one risks repeating the cycle of overpromising and disappointment that has paralyzed American nuclear waste policy for four decades.

I say this as a former Energy Department official who served as federal manager for the Consent-Based Siting Consortia — a $24 million 12-team initiative supporting public engagement around the siting of spent-fuel storage facilities. Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan must clear five tests.

First, the department must explain the scale of its projections. Its January solicitation offered an illustrative scenario in which one campus employed 50,000 direct workers, generated another 100,000 to 150,000 indirect jobs, and required 10,000 to 20,000 housing units. The same document put the entire existing U.S. nuclear workforce at roughly 80,000. By July, the Energy Department was projecting 25,000 jobs per campus .

Those figures may rest on different assumptions, but the Energy Department has not explained the methodology or reconciled the difference. Numbers that swing this far before a single site is chosen are aspirations, not plans.

Second, the department needs a technically credible schedule. Its solicitation says it wants initial facilities online “in the 2027 timeframe” and promises preference to the states with “more ambitious timelines” — remarkably soon for infrastructure of this kind.

States, meanwhile, had just nine weeks to assemble sweeping proposals. Any serious schedule for the waste disposition component must separately account for geological screening, independent site characterization, groundwater and seismic studies, environmental review, Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing, transportation planning and host-agreement negotiation. A facility built to isolate waste for decades, centuries, or millennia cannot be validated on a ribbon-cutting schedule.

Third, Washington must put up real money and enforceable commitments. A repository would, in principle, draw on the federal Nuclear Waste Fund . But for nearly everything else, the department told states to look to private capital — industry, technology firms, private equity, venture funds. It floats possible federal cost-sharing, loan guarantees and grants, but it commits to none and says states and private investors are expected to lead and finance the effort.

Communities asked to keep nuclear waste for generations need money that is committed and obligations that are enforceable against future administrations.

Fourth, Congress must authorize the plan’s spent-fuel storage and disposal components. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act still directs the federal repository program toward Yucca Mountain, whose development Congress has not funded since fiscal 2010 . The act also prevents construction of a centralized federal spent fuel storage facility until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has authorized construction of a repository. The department cannot designate one of the five states as a spent fuel site by press release.

Fifth, host communities must consent. States applied and governors signed, and some local governments in Utah, Idaho and Tennessee have expressed preliminary support. But it is far from clear that any specific community has agreed to live beside nuclear waste facilities.

Genuine consent requires a named candidate community, early involvement rather than after-the-fact persuasion, meaningful say over benefits, the participation of affected Tribal Nations and a real chance to walk away before commitments are final. The Energy Department’s process ran the other way: It gave states nine weeks to name sites and gauge local sentiment and rewarded those promising to streamline permitting and move fast.

After decades in which states treated nuclear waste as politically untouchable, the willingness of five governors to enter the negotiating room is a real achievement. But no spent-fuel repository in any of the five states is authorized under current law, no community has completed a voluntary siting process, no binding host agreement has been signed and no durable financing package or credible schedule has been demonstrated.

When a willing community stays at the table through investigation, negotiation, licensing and construction, the Energy Department will have earned its victory lap. For now, it has earned only the right to begin the hard work of getting there.

Vincent Ialenti is a former U.S. Department of Energy official and a senior research fellow at Tampere University in Finland. He is the author of “Deep Time Reckoning” and “Longstorming,” both from MIT Press.
